source: Written 2026-10-23/24 by Claude Sonnet from our own summaries of the NC 2017 standards, and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin.

notes.NC17.M3.N-CN.9: Questions state "real coefficients" wherever conjugate pairs or odd-degree facts are used. "Roots" are counted with multiplicity unless the stem says "different". Nothing needs a calculator or factoring beyond simple quadratics and one given root.
notes.NC17.M3.A-SSE.1: Expressions are interpreted from their written form; every piecewise rule is given in words and no graph is referred to. Several options are phrases, not numbers, so a few choice keys are longer than a bare number would be; lengths were balanced across the part. Graph-based interpretation is replaced by verbal descriptions and formulas; no figure is referred to. Rational expressions are read by their parts, their undefined values and their behavior for large inputs described in words.
notes.NC17.M3.A-SSE.2: Full 69 written (23 per difficulty). Choice stems that ask for a complete factorization say so; rounded numeric answers have no compute.
notes.NC17.M3.A-SSE.3: The standard is often taught with a calculator (for example 1.15^t written as about 1.012^(12t)). These are written to be exact by hand: bases are perfect powers (4, 8, 9, 16, 27, 1.21, 1.44, 0.81) or the rewritten form is left as a power. Only one question needs rounding-free decimal arithmetic (600 times 1.0404). Only exact, hand-computable questions; no approximations needed except the one question that says to round.
notes.NC17.M3.A-APR.2: All questions are answerable by hand with the Remainder Theorem (evaluating p(a), including a = -a for x + a and a = b/a for ax - b). Skills are spread over seven kinds: remainder by evaluating, factor test, unknown coefficient, divisors x + a and ax - b, the division statement, interpreting a remainder, and finding other zeros from a known factor.
notes.NC17.M3.A-APR.3: Questions stay on the link between factors, zeros and solutions; the remainder theorem and polynomial division as such (neighbouring standards) are avoided. Graphs are described by their zeros only.
notes.NC17.M3.A-APR.6: Divisors are linear (leading coefficient 1 or 2) or quadratic, as a "simple rational expression"; the quotients always have integer coefficients. The remainder theorem appears only as a shortcut for a remainder value (3 questions).
notes.NC17.M3.A-CED.1: Covers absolute value, polynomial, exponential and rational equations and inequalities, written from situations and solved algebraically; graphical solving is asked through where graphs cross and a table of values, since a graph cannot be shown.
notes.NC17.M3.A-CED.2: Graphs are described by features and equations, never shown. 16 choice (writing an equation is a choice), 14 numeric. Skills: absolute value write (3) and read (4), polynomial write (4), evaluate and read (3) and end behavior (1), exponential write (4) and evaluate and read (4), rational write (3) and read asymptotes and intercepts (4).
notes.NC17.M3.A-REI.1: Justifying steps is mostly verbal, so about two thirds of these are choice questions (which property, which reason, which error). The number questions ask for a step number, the number used in a step, or a value that a step changes, so each still has one exact answer.
notes.NC17.M3.A-REI.2: Numeric answers are limited to one valid solution; extraneous roots are asked as choice questions or as a count of solutions. No graphing technology is used.
notes.NC17.M3.A-REI.11: Graphs and technology are replaced by intersection points given in words and by written-out tables of values, with continuous functions assumed. Skills: why an intersection solves f(x) = g(x) (4), read solutions from intersection points (6), find a solution from a table (6), check a solution in both functions (4), count solutions from the intersections (5), choose the two graphs for an equation (5). Approximating by tables is asked as: x-value where outputs are closest, sign change between two x-values, or the matching row.
notes.NC17.M3.F-IF.1: Acute angles from 0 to 90 degrees only (right-triangle ratios as functions); no unit circle or periodicity. Technology is not needed: exact values come from the special triangles, and non-special values are given in the question.
notes.NC17.M3.F-IF.2: Piecewise functions are written in words and plain math (no cases environment). Every question has a single valid answer: for "find x" questions only one piece gives an input inside its own domain. Contexts use dollars written in words.
notes.NC17.M3.F-IF.4: NC Math 3: graphs are described by features in words, or by short tables. Period, midline and amplitude questions use exact values, and discontinuities are asked by formula (holes, asymptotes), by a described break (jump) or by a step-function story.
notes.NC17.M3.F-IF.7: Graphs are described by equations, tables of features and words, since no picture can be shown. Piecewise 4, absolute value 4, polynomial 6, exponential 4, rational 6, sine/cosine 6.
notes.NC17.M3.F-IF.9: Each question gives one function as an equation and the other as a table, a short description of its graph, or words, never as a picture. Graphs are described by their features (intercepts, vertex, highest and lowest values, asymptotes).
notes.NC17.M3.F-BF.1: Thirty questions: exponentials from points and descriptions, polynomials from zeros, vertex or points, and sums, differences, products and quotients of functions in context. Graphs are given as zeros, vertex and points in words.
notes.NC17.M3.F-BF.4: Inverses of linear, quadratic (restricted domain) and exponential functions, with context; whether an inverse exists is asked from formulas, lists of pairs and reasons. Graph reflection is asked through swapped points only.
notes.NC17.M3.F-LE.3: Written for NC Math 3 as hand-checkable comparisons: tables of values, average rates of change over equal intervals, smallest-x crossing questions with exact integer powers, and choice questions about which function eventually exceeds another. Graphs are not used.
notes.NC17.M3.F-LE.4: Evaluation with technology is asked as a rounded decimal (a calculator is assumed) and compute is left empty for those, since logarithms cannot be written in the checker's expression language. Exact-form answers are choice questions.
notes.NC17.M3.F-TF.1: Answers containing pi are choice questions; numeric ones use plain numbers or 3.14 where stated.
notes.NC17.M3.F-TF.2: Tables and graphs are written out as lists of values or as features (zeros, period, greatest value); technology is not asked. Irrational values are choice questions, so about half the set is choice.
notes.NC17.M3.F-TF.5: Technology is replaced by hand work: reading amplitude, period, midline and extremes from f(x) = a sin(bx) + h, writing the equation from features, interpreting and evaluating models at exact angles. Radian measure throughout.
notes.NC17.M3.G-CO.11: Proof work is asked as choice questions about the reasons in a written argument, plus numeric questions that use the theorems (algebra, perimeter, coordinates).
notes.NC17.M3.G-CO.14: Proofs are asked as choice questions about a written argument (the reason for a step, the statement that completes it); problem solving is numeric. Figures are triangles and quadrilaterals only; circles belong to other standards. Coordinates appear in a few questions on which figure a quadrilateral is.
notes.NC17.M3.G-C.2: Thirty questions on central, inscribed, tangent-chord, chord-chord and secant angles; tangent and radius; tangent segments; chords and the center; segment products. Circles are described in words, no figures. Proof of the theorems is not asked.
notes.NC17.M3.G-C.5: Answers with pi in them are choice questions; numeric ones use k pi with k asked for, or 3.14 as the value of pi. Questions are about arc length, radian measure and sector area; converting between degrees and radians as a skill is a separate standard and is not tested on its own.
notes.NC17.M3.G-GPE.1: Derivation of the equation is asked through the Pythagorean Theorem (legs |x-h| and |y-k|, hypotenuse r) as choice and numeric questions; completing the square is asked for center and radius separately, including a leading coefficient and a fractional center.
notes.NC17.M3.G-GMD.3: Answers with pi are choice questions (in terms of pi); numeric ones use a stated 3.14, rational volumes, or reverse problems. Formulas are not given in the stems.
notes.NC17.M3.G-GMD.4: Text-only: every solid, plane and rotation is described in words and lengths. About half the set is naming (cross-sections and solids of rotation); the rest asks for a length or an area so that each can be computed exactly.
notes.NC17.M3.G-MG.1: Answers that involve pi are choice questions or give a value for pi (3.14 or 3); all optimization is done on a given quadratic or a short list of candidates, by hand. Density is covered for mass and for population.
notes.NC17.M3.S-IC.1: Inference from a random sample is tested through estimates (proportion, count, mean) and through choice questions on random vs biased selection, sampling variability, and what a result supports. Simulation and margin of error are not part of the summary and are not asked.
notes.NC17.M3.S-IC.3: A conceptual standard, so most questions are choice (25 of 30) and the numeric ones count group or sample sizes under a random design. Designs are asked about only in outline (random selection, random assignment, matched pairs, systematic and proportional sampling), not as calculations of probability or inference.
notes.NC17.M3.S-IC.4: Simulation is asked by hand: simulated results are given as lists or summary statistics (SD, mean) and the margin of error is two standard deviations or 2*sqrt(p(1-p)/n), with the method stated in each stem.
notes.NC17.M3.S-IC.5: Hand-answerable simulation only: simulated results are given as counts, ranges or short lists, since students cannot run a simulation in text.
notes.NC17.M3.S-IC.6: Articles, websites and graphs cannot be shown, so each is described in words and the student judges the source, the design or the display. Where a check can be made exactly (a percent change, a truncated axis, a median, a mean) the question is numeric.

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: How many complex roots does the polynomial $x^5 - 3x + 1$ have, counting repeated roots?
questions.solution: By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, a polynomial of degree 5 has exactly 5 complex roots, counting repeated roots.

solve.work: Degree 5, so by the FTA exactly 5 complex roots counting multiplicity.

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: A polynomial has degree 7. Which statement about its complex roots, counting multiplicity, must be true?
questions.solution: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says a polynomial of degree 7 has exactly 7 complex roots, counting multiplicity. They need not all be real.

solve.work: FTA: degree 7 means exactly 7 complex roots counting multiplicity. Not necessarily all real.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: How many roots, counting repeats, does $(x-2)^3(x+1)$ have?
questions.solution: The factor $(x-2)^3$ gives the root 2 three times and $(x+1)$ gives $-1$ once, so there are $3 + 1 = 4$ roots.

questions.skill: Find the missing roots
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 3 has the roots 2 and $-5$, each used once. How many more roots does it have, counting repeats?
questions.solution: It has 3 roots in all, and 2 are known, so $3 - 2 = 1$ more root.

solve.work: Degree 3 gives 3 roots; 2 are known, so 1 more.

questions.skill: Conjugate pairs of nonreal roots
questions.stem: A polynomial with real coefficients has $2 + 3i$ as a root. Which number must also be a root?
questions.solution: For a polynomial with real coefficients, nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs. The conjugate of $2 + 3i$ is $2 - 3i$.

solve.work: Real coefficients: nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs, so 2 - 3i.

questions.skill: Quadratic roots and the discriminant
questions.stem: How many real roots does $x^2 + 9 = 0$ have?
questions.solution: Solving gives $x^2 = -9$, and no real number squares to a negative number. The roots are $3i$ and $-3i$, so there are no real roots.

solve.work: x^2 = -9, x = 3i or -3i. No real roots: 0.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: Which list gives all the roots of $(x+2)^2(x-7)$, counting repeats?
questions.solution: $(x+2)^2 = 0$ gives $x = -2$ twice, and $x - 7 = 0$ gives $x = 7$. The roots are $-2, -2, 7$.

questions.skill: Roots and x-intercepts
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 5 has at most ? x-intercepts. What number is the ?
questions.solution: Each x-intercept is a real root, and a polynomial of degree 5 has only 5 roots in all, so it has at most 5 x-intercepts.

solve.work: A degree 5 polynomial has at most 5 real roots, so at most 5 x-intercepts.

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: Which polynomial has exactly 6 complex roots, counting multiplicity?
questions.solution: The number of complex roots equals the degree. $x^6 - 1$ has degree 6.

solve.work: Degrees: 12, 3, 6, 1. Only x^6 - 1 has degree 6, so 6 roots.

questions.skill: Odd degree has a real root
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 3 with real coefficients must have at least how many real roots?
questions.solution: Nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs, so the number of nonreal roots is even. Out of 3 roots, at most 2 can be nonreal, so at least 1 is real.

solve.work: Nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs; 3 roots cannot all pair up, so at least 1 real root.

questions.skill: Find the missing roots
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 2 with real coefficients has the root $4i$. What is its other root?
questions.solution: Nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs. With degree 2, the other root is the conjugate of $4i$, which is $-4i$.

solve.work: Nonreal roots of real-coefficient polynomials come in conjugate pairs: -4i.

questions.skill: Smallest degree from given roots
questions.stem: What is the smallest possible degree of a polynomial that has the roots $1$, $2$ and $3$?
questions.solution: Each different root needs its own factor, and three factors make degree 3.

solve.work: (x-1)(x-2)(x-3) has degree 3; fewer degrees cannot have 3 distinct roots.

questions.skill: Odd degree has a real root
questions.stem: A polynomial has real coefficients. Which degree guarantees that it has at least one real root?
questions.solution: Nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs, so their number is even. An odd degree such as 7 leaves at least one real root. Degrees 2, 4 and 6 can have all roots nonreal.

solve.work: Odd degree real polynomial must cross the x-axis; degree 7.

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, how many complex roots, counting multiplicity, does $f(x) = 4x^{3} - x^{2} + 6$ have?
questions.solution: The degree is 3 (the highest power of $x$), so there are 3 complex roots, counting multiplicity. The coefficient 4 does not change the count.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: What is the multiplicity of the root $x = 2$ in $(x-2)^{3}(x+5)^{2}$?
questions.solution: The factor $(x-2)$ appears 3 times, so the root 2 has multiplicity 3.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: A polynomial has the root 7 with multiplicity 3 and the root 0 with multiplicity 1, and no other roots. What is its degree?
questions.solution: The degree is the number of roots, counting multiplicity: $3 + 1 = 4$.

questions.skill: Quadratic roots and the discriminant
questions.stem: What is the discriminant, $b^{2} - 4ac$, of $x^{2} + 2x + 5$?

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: What does the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra say about a polynomial of degree $n$, where $n \ge 1$?
choices: It has exactly $n$ real roots, counting multiplicity.
It has exactly $n$ complex roots, counting multiplicity.
It has exactly one complex root, whatever the degree is.
It has at most $n - 1$ complex roots, counting multiplicity.
questions.answer: It has exactly $n$ complex roots, counting multiplicity.
questions.solution: A polynomial of degree $n \ge 1$ has exactly $n$ complex roots when repeated roots are counted. They need not be real.

solve.answer: It has exactly $n$ complex roots, counting multiplicity.
solve.work: FTA: a degree-n polynomial (n>=1) has exactly n complex roots counting multiplicity.

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: How many solutions in the complex numbers, counting repeats, does $x^{8} - 2x + 5 = 0$ have?
questions.solution: By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, a polynomial equation of degree 8 has 8 complex solutions, counting repeats.

solve.work: Degree 8 polynomial: by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra it has 8 complex solutions counting multiplicity.

questions.skill: Solutions of a power equation
questions.stem: Which are all the solutions of $x^{2} = -16$ in the complex numbers?
questions.solution: $(4i)^{2} = 16i^{2} = -16$ and $(-4i)^{2} = -16$. The equation has degree 2, so these two are all the solutions.

solve.work: x^2 = -16 gives x = +/- sqrt(-16) = +/- 4i. Both 4i and -4i.

questions.skill: Quadratic roots and the discriminant
questions.stem: Which quadratic equation has two nonreal roots?
questions.solution: Two nonreal roots need a negative discriminant. For $x^{2} + 2x + 3$ it is $4 - 12 = -8$. The others have discriminants 1, 0 and 25.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: How many roots, counting repeats, does $3x(x-4)^{2}$ have?
questions.solution: The factor $x$ gives the root 0 once and $(x-4)^{2}$ gives the root 4 twice. That is $1 + 2 = 3$ roots.

solve.work: Degree 3 (3x times quadratic): roots 0, 4, 4. Counting repeats: 3.

questions.skill: Roots and x-intercepts
questions.stem: The roots of a polynomial with real coefficients are $2$, $-1$, $4i$ and $-4i$. How many x-intercepts does its graph have?
questions.solution: Only real roots are x-intercepts. The real roots are 2 and $-1$, so there are 2.

solve.work: Real roots 2 and -1 are x-intercepts; 4i, -4i are not real. 2 intercepts.

questions.skill: Conjugate pairs of nonreal roots
questions.stem: Which pair could be the nonreal roots of a polynomial with real coefficients?
questions.solution: Nonreal roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs $a + bi$ and $a - bi$. Only $2 + i$ and $2 - i$ are conjugates.

solve.work: Nonreal roots of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs: 2+i and 2-i.

questions.skill: Spot a true statement
questions.stem: Which statement is true for every polynomial of degree 4 with real coefficients?
choices: It has exactly 4 complex roots, counting multiplicity.
It has exactly 4 different roots, one for each factor.
It has exactly 4 real roots, counting multiplicity.
It has at least 2 real roots, counting multiplicity.
questions.answer: It has exactly 4 complex roots, counting multiplicity.
questions.solution: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra gives 4 roots counting multiplicity. They need not be different or real; for example, $x^{4} + 1$ has no real roots.

solve.answer: It has exactly 4 complex roots, counting multiplicity.
solve.work: By the Fundamental Theorem, degree 4 means exactly 4 complex roots counting multiplicity. x^4+1 has no real roots, so A and D fail; (x-1)^4 has one distinct root, so C fails.

questions.skill: Possible numbers of real and nonreal roots
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 7 has real coefficients and exactly 6 nonreal roots, counting multiplicity. How many real roots does it have, counting multiplicity?
questions.solution: There are 7 roots in all, so $7 - 6 = 1$ is real.

solve.work: Degree 7 means 7 roots counting multiplicity; 7 - 6 = 1 real root.

questions.skill: Conjugate pairs of nonreal roots
questions.stem: The polynomial $f$ has real coefficients, and $f(3 - i) = 0$. Which other number must also satisfy $f(x) = 0$?
questions.solution: Nonreal roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs, so the conjugate of $3 - i$, which is $3 + i$, must also be a root.

solve.work: Real coefficients: conjugate 3+i is a root.

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: A polynomial has exactly 5 complex roots, counting multiplicity, and no other roots. What is its degree?
questions.solution: The number of complex roots, counting multiplicity, equals the degree, so the degree is 5.

solve.work: Degree equals number of roots with multiplicity: 5.

questions.skill: Roots and x-intercepts
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 4 has real coefficients and 4 different real roots. How many x-intercepts does its graph have?
questions.solution: Each real root is an x-intercept, so there are 4.

solve.work: 4 distinct real roots each give an x-intercept: 4.

questions.skill: Solutions of a power equation
questions.stem: Which equation has exactly 3 complex solutions, counting repeats?
questions.solution: The number of solutions equals the degree. Only $x^{3} - 8 = 0$ has degree 3.

questions.skill: Solutions of a power equation
questions.stem: How many solutions in the complex numbers does $x^{4} = 81$ have?
questions.solution: $x^{4} - 81 = 0$ has degree 4, so it has 4 complex solutions. They are $3$, $-3$, $3i$ and $-3i$.

questions.skill: Possible numbers of real and nonreal roots
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 6 has real coefficients and no real roots at all. Into how many conjugate pairs do its 6 nonreal roots fall?
questions.solution: Nonreal roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs, so 6 nonreal roots make $6 \div 2 = 3$ pairs.

solve.work: 6 nonreal roots in conjugate pairs: 3 pairs.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: Which polynomial has $-3$ as a root with multiplicity 2?
questions.solution: The root $-3$ comes from the factor $(x+3)$, and multiplicity 2 means that factor is squared. Only the first has $(x+3)^{2}$.

solve.work: (x+3)^2 gives root -3 with multiplicity 2: (x+3)^2(x-1). (x+3)^3 x has multiplicity 3.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: How many different numbers are roots of $(x-4)^2(x+1)(x-6)^2$?
questions.solution: The roots are 4, $-1$ and 6. The repeats do not add new numbers, so there are 3 different roots.

questions.skill: Possible numbers of real and nonreal roots
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 4 with real coefficients has exactly 2 real roots, counting multiplicity. How many of its complex roots are not real?
questions.solution: It has 4 roots in all, and 2 are real, so $4 - 2 = 2$ are not real. They form one conjugate pair.

solve.work: Degree 4 gives 4 roots; 2 real, so 4 - 2 = 2 nonreal.

questions.skill: Conjugate pairs of nonreal roots
questions.stem: A cubic polynomial with real coefficients has the roots $4$ and $1 - 5i$. What is the third root?
questions.solution: The nonreal root $1 - 5i$ needs its conjugate $1 + 5i$ as a root too. That makes three roots: $4$, $1 - 5i$ and $1 + 5i$.

solve.work: Conjugate of 1 - 5i is 1 + 5i, which must be the third root.

questions.skill: Smallest degree from given roots
questions.stem: A polynomial with real coefficients has the roots $2$, $-1$ and $3 + i$. What is the smallest possible degree of the polynomial?
questions.solution: Since $3 + i$ is a root, its conjugate $3 - i$ is also a root. The roots $2$, $-1$, $3 + i$ and $3 - i$ make at least 4, so the degree is at least 4.

solve.work: Roots 2, -1, 3+i, and conjugate 3-i must also be a root: at least 4 roots, smallest degree 4.

questions.skill: Odd degree has a real root
questions.stem: Which polynomial with real coefficients must have at least one real root?
questions.solution: A polynomial of odd degree has an odd number of roots, and nonreal roots come in pairs, so at least one root is real. The others have even degree and no real roots, since each of $x^4$, $x^2$ and $x^6$ is at least 0.

solve.work: Odd degree with real coefficients must have a real root: x^5 + 2x^2 + 1. The others are always positive (x^4+3x^2+1, x^2+4, x^4+1 > 0).

questions.skill: Possible numbers of real and nonreal roots
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 5 has real coefficients. Which could be its number of nonreal complex roots, counting multiplicity?
questions.solution: Nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs, so their number is even. Of the choices 3, 5, 1 and 4, only 4 is even. A polynomial with 4 nonreal roots and degree 5 has 1 real root.

solve.work: Nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs, so their count is even and at most 5: 0, 2 or 4. Among the options only 4.

questions.skill: Quadratic roots and the discriminant
questions.stem: Which describes the roots of $x^2 - 6x + 13 = 0$?
questions.solution: The discriminant is $(-6)^2 - 4(1)(13) = 36 - 52 = -16$, which is negative. So there are two nonreal complex roots, which are conjugates.

questions.skill: Find the missing roots
questions.stem: A polynomial of degree 4 has real coefficients and the roots $1 + i$ and $-3i$. What are the other two roots?
questions.solution: Each nonreal root needs its conjugate. The conjugate of $1 + i$ is $1 - i$, and the conjugate of $-3i$ is $3i$. Together with the two given roots, that is all 4.

solve.work: Conjugates of 1 + i and -3i are 1 - i and 3i.

questions.skill: Spot a false statement
questions.stem: Which statement is false for a polynomial of degree 6 with real coefficients?
choices: It always has 6 different real roots.
It has exactly 6 complex roots, counting multiplicity.
It can have no real roots.
questions.answer: It always has 6 different real roots.
questions.solution: A polynomial of degree 6 can have nonreal roots or repeated roots, so it need not have 6 different real roots. For example, $x^6 + 1$ has no real roots.

solve.answer: It always has 6 different real roots.
solve.work: "Always has 6 different real roots" is false (e.g. x^6 + 1 has none). The others are true.

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: How many roots, counting repeats, does $x^3(x-2)^2(x+5)$ have?
questions.solution: The root 0 is used 3 times, the root 2 twice and the root $-5$ once: $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$. This also matches the degree, 6.

questions.skill: Roots and x-intercepts
questions.stem: How many nonreal roots, counting multiplicity, does $x^{4} - 16$ have?
questions.solution: $x^{4} - 16 = (x^{2} - 4)(x^{2} + 4)$. The real roots are 2 and $-2$, and the other two roots, $2i$ and $-2i$, are nonreal.

questions.skill: Number of roots from the degree
questions.stem: Which equation has exactly 6 complex solutions, counting multiplicity?
questions.solution: The number of solutions is the degree. The degrees are $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$, $2 + 3 = 5$, $2 + 2 + 1 = 5$ and $2 + 2 = 4$.

questions.skill: Quadratic roots and the discriminant
questions.stem: For the quadratic $x^{2} - 8x + c$ to have two nonreal roots, $c$ must be greater than what number?
questions.solution: The discriminant $64 - 4c$ must be negative, so $c > 16$.

solve.work: Nonreal roots need discriminant 64-4c<0, i.e. c>16.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: What are all the roots, counting multiplicity, of $x^{2}(x-3)(x+2)^{2}$?
questions.solution: $x^{2}$ gives 0 twice, $(x-3)$ gives 3 once and $(x+2)^{2}$ gives $-2$ twice.

questions.skill: Solutions of a power equation
questions.stem: How many nonreal solutions does $x^{6} = 64$ have?
questions.solution: The equation has 6 complex solutions. Two are real, 2 and $-2$, so $6 - 2 = 4$ are nonreal.

solve.work: x^6 = 64: six roots 2e^{ikπ/3}, k=0..5. Real: 2 and -2. Nonreal: 4.

questions.skill: Spot a true statement
questions.stem: Maria says a polynomial of degree 3 with real coefficients can have 3 nonreal roots. Is she right?
choices: Yes, because there are 3 roots and any of them can be nonreal.
No, because nonreal roots come in pairs and 3 is odd.
Yes, if the three roots are conjugates of one another.
No, because every cubic has exactly three real roots.
questions.answer: No, because nonreal roots come in pairs and 3 is odd.
questions.solution: With real coefficients, nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs, so there are an even number of them. A cubic can have 0 or 2 nonreal roots, never 3.

solve.answer: No, because nonreal roots come in pairs and 3 is odd.
solve.work: With real coefficients, nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs, so a cubic has at most 2 nonreal roots and at least one real root.

questions.skill: Quadratic roots and the discriminant
questions.stem: A quadratic with real coefficients has a discriminant of $-7$. Which describes its roots?
choices: Two nonreal roots that are not conjugates
questions.solution: A negative discriminant gives two nonreal roots, and for real coefficients they are conjugates $a + bi$ and $a - bi$.

solve.work: Negative discriminant with real coefficients: two nonreal conjugate roots.

questions.skill: Roots from factored form
questions.stem: How many real roots, counting multiplicity, does $(x^{2}+4)(x-5)^{2}(x+1)$ have?
questions.solution: $x^{2} + 4 = 0$ has only nonreal roots. The real roots are 5 twice and $-1$ once, so there are 3.

solve.work: x^2+4 has no real roots; (x-5)^2 gives 2; (x+1) gives 1; total 3.
