Only Study X shows a real difference, because Y's count is not 0
Neither study can show a real difference, since both counts are above 0
questions.answer: Both suggest a real difference, but Study X gives stronger evidence
questions.solution: Study X is 0.2% and Study Y is 4%, so both are below 5%. The smaller the proportion, the stronger the evidence, so X is stronger.

solve.answer: Both suggest a real difference, but Study X gives stronger evidence
solve.work: X: 0.2%, Y: 4%; both below 5%, X stronger.

questions.skill: Tell a real difference from an important one
questions.stem: A very large experiment finds that students using a new app scored 0.1 point higher on a 100-point test. In a simulation, only 1 of 10,000 trials gave a difference that large. Which is the best statement?
choices: Chance is a likely explanation, since a difference of 0.1 point is so very small
Chance is an unlikely explanation, but 0.1 point may be too small to matter
The app must matter greatly, because the simulation result is so very rare
The simulation is flawed, since it cannot give such a small count of trials
questions.answer: Chance is an unlikely explanation, but 0.1 point may be too small to matter
questions.solution: The simulation says the difference is probably not chance, but a rare result does not mean a large one. 0.1 point on a 100-point test may be of no practical importance.

solve.answer: Chance is an unlikely explanation, but 0.1 point may be too small to matter
solve.work: 1 in 10,000 makes chance unlikely, but 0.1 point on 100 may have no practical importance.

questions.skill: Judge the source of the data
questions.stem: An article says a new snack is good for your health. The study it cites was paid for by the company that makes the snack. What is the best reason to be careful about the article's claim?
choices: Companies are not allowed to pay for studies of their snacks
The study was probably too recent for its results to count yet
The company may gain if the results make the snack look good
Snack studies never include enough people to show anything
questions.answer: The company may gain if the results make the snack look good
questions.solution: A source that gains from the result may, even without meaning to, design the study or report the results in its own favor. That does not prove the claim false, but it is a reason to look for independent evidence. The other reasons are not true in general.

solve.answer: The company may gain if the results make the snack look good
solve.work: Funding by the maker is a conflict of interest: the company gains if the snack looks healthy.

questions.skill: Judge how a sample was chosen
questions.stem: A website asks visitors to vote on whether the town should build a new park. Of those who vote, 90% say yes. Why can't we conclude that 90% of the town's residents want the park?
choices: Only people who chose to vote are counted, and they may differ
The poll was open on a weekday, when most residents are busy working
Ninety percent is too large a share to be possible in a poll
Residents of a town never visit websites to vote on things
questions.answer: Only people who chose to vote are counted, and they may differ
questions.solution: A voluntary poll includes only people who chose to take part. They are often the people with the strongest views, and they may not represent all residents.

solve.answer: Only people who chose to vote are counted, and they may differ
solve.work: Self-selected voters (voluntary response) may differ from residents overall.

questions.skill: Check a report's claim against its numbers
questions.stem: A store's ad says, "Sales jumped 50%!" The store sold 20 items last week and 24 items this week. By what percent did sales actually increase?
questions.solution: The increase is $24 - 20 = 4$ items, and $\frac{4}{20} = 0.20$, which is 20%. The ad's 50% is not supported by the numbers.

solve.work: Increase 24-20=4; 4/20=0.20 = 20%. Ad claim of 50% is false.

questions.skill: Spot a misleading graph axis or scale
questions.stem: A bar graph's vertical axis starts at 50 instead of 0. What effect does this have on how the graph looks?
choices: Differences between bars look smaller than they really are
Every bar is drawn twice as tall as it should be
The order of the bars from tallest to shortest changes
Differences between bars look bigger than they really are
questions.answer: Differences between bars look bigger than they really are
questions.solution: When the axis is cut off, the bars show only the part above 50. A small difference then looks like a big one. The order of the bars does not change.

solve.answer: Differences between bars look bigger than they really are
solve.work: Truncated axis exaggerates differences between bars.

questions.skill: Judge the source of the data
questions.stem: Which source is the best choice for the number of people living in a large city?
choices: A post by a stranger on a popular social media site
A national census office's published report
An advertisement for a moving company in that city
A blog that does not say where its numbers come from
questions.answer: A national census office's published report
questions.solution: A census office collects its counts carefully and publishes how it did so. The others do not say where their numbers come from or may have a reason to change them.

solve.answer: A national census office's published report
solve.work: A national census office is the authoritative, documented source.

questions.skill: Judge how a sample was chosen
questions.stem: A cafe says, "75% of customers love our new menu!" It asked only the first 8 customers of the day. How many of those 8 customers loved the menu?
questions.solution: $75\%$ of 8 is $0.75 \cdot 8 = 6$. A claim based on only 8 people is weak evidence about all customers.

questions.skill: Judge a study design and its conclusion
questions.stem: A study finds that students who eat breakfast have higher test scores. A headline says, "Breakfast raises test scores." What is wrong with the headline?
choices: Test scores cannot be measured reliably in any kind of study
Breakfast has no effect on test scores for any student
The study only observed students, so it cannot show cause
The study should have asked the teachers for their opinions
questions.answer: The study only observed students, so it cannot show cause
questions.solution: In an observational study, other differences between the groups (such as sleep or family income) could explain the scores. Only a well-designed experiment can support a claim of cause and effect.

solve.answer: The study only observed students, so it cannot show cause
solve.work: Observational study shows association, not causation.

questions.skill: Judge a summary or picture display
questions.stem: A pie chart's labels read 40%, 35% and 25% for three parts, plus a fourth part labeled 30%. What does this tell you?
choices: The percentages add to more than 100%, so the chart has an error
The chart is correct, because every one of its parts is under 50%
The fourth part must be the largest part of the whole pie
The chart shows only some of the people who were surveyed
questions.answer: The percentages add to more than 100%, so the chart has an error
questions.solution: The parts of a pie chart must add to 100%. Here $40 + 35 + 25 + 30 = 130$, so something is wrong and the chart should not be trusted as drawn.

solve.answer: The percentages add to more than 100%, so the chart has an error
solve.work: 40+35+25+30=130% > 100%, so the chart has an error.

questions.skill: Judge the source of the data
questions.stem: A report gives some striking numbers but does not say who collected the data or how. What should a careful reader do?
choices: Trust the numbers, because exact numbers are always accurate
Trust the numbers if the report is long and well written
Ignore all of the numbers that are small or round
Look for the original source before trusting the numbers
questions.answer: Look for the original source before trusting the numbers
questions.solution: Without knowing who collected the data and how, there is no way to judge its quality. A careful reader looks for the original source.

solve.answer: Look for the original source before trusting the numbers
solve.work: Unknown source: find the original source before trusting.

questions.skill: Judge how a sample was chosen
questions.stem: A survey about a new library asks, "Don't you agree that the wonderful new library is worth the cost?" Why is this question a problem?
choices: It asks about a library instead of asking about a school
Its wording pushes people toward answering yes
It does not allow people to give a numeric answer
It is much too short to be answered in a fair way
questions.answer: Its wording pushes people toward answering yes
questions.solution: A leading question is worded to push people toward one answer. A fair question uses neutral words, such as "Do you support or oppose building a new library?"

solve.answer: Its wording pushes people toward answering yes
solve.work: Leading, loaded wording pushes toward yes.

questions.skill: Spot a misleading graph axis or scale
questions.stem: A bar graph of two test averages has a vertical axis that starts at 80. The bars show averages of 84 and 88. The taller bar is drawn how many times as tall as the shorter bar?
questions.solution: The visible heights are measured from 80: $84 - 80 = 4$ and $88 - 80 = 8$. The taller bar is drawn $\frac{8}{4} = 2$ times as tall, although 88 is only about 1.05 times 84.

questions.skill: Judge how a sample was chosen
questions.stem: A principal wants to know what all students think about a new lunch menu. Which way of choosing students gives the best picture?
choices: Ask the first 50 students who reach the cafeteria
Ask the 50 students on the school's cooking club
Choose 50 students at random from the school roster
Ask the 50 students who reply to an online poll
questions.answer: Choose 50 students at random from the school roster
questions.solution: A random sample from the full roster gives every student a chance to be chosen, so it is likely to represent the school. The other groups choose themselves or are special.

solve.answer: Choose 50 students at random from the school roster
solve.work: A simple random sample from the roster represents all students.

questions.skill: Judge the source of the data
questions.stem: Which information would most help you judge whether the source of a report's data is reliable?
choices: Who collected the data and whether they gain from the results
How many different colors are used in the graphs of the report
How long the report is, counted in pages and words
How many other websites have a link to the report
questions.answer: Who collected the data and whether they gain from the results
questions.solution: Reliability depends on who gathered the data, the method used, and any reason the gatherer has to favor a result. Style and length do not tell you that.

solve.answer: Who collected the data and whether they gain from the results
solve.work: Who collected the data and whether they gain judges reliability.

questions.skill: Check a report's claim against its numbers
questions.stem: A report says, "The crime rate fell from 8% to 6%, a drop of only 2." By what percent did the crime rate actually fall?
questions.solution: The drop is $8 - 6 = 2$ percentage points. Compared with the starting rate, $\frac{2}{8} = 0.25$, so the rate fell by 25%. A drop of "only 2" hides how large the change is.

questions.skill: Judge a study design and its conclusion
questions.stem: To decide whether a new tutoring program raises scores, which design gives the strongest evidence?
choices: Compare students who chose the program with the students who did not
Ask students afterward whether they liked the program
Compare this year's scores with scores from ten years ago
Randomly assign students to the program or to a comparison group
questions.answer: Randomly assign students to the program or to a comparison group
questions.solution: Random assignment makes the groups alike on average, so a difference in scores can be traced to the program. Self-selected groups and old comparisons have other differences.

solve.answer: Randomly assign students to the program or to a comparison group
solve.work: Random assignment to treatment/comparison is a randomized experiment, strongest evidence.

questions.skill: Spot a misleading graph axis or scale
questions.stem: A line graph has equally spaced marks on the horizontal axis labeled 2010, 2011, 2012, 2016 and 2020. What is misleading about it?
choices: The years are not listed in order from least to greatest
The gaps between years are unequal, so slopes are distorted
A line graph cannot be used to show a change in years
The marks make the graph look much longer than needed
questions.answer: The gaps between years are unequal, so slopes are distorted
questions.solution: Equal spacing on the axis suggests equal time between points, but the gaps are 1, 1, 4 and 4 years. The slope of each segment then misrepresents the rate of change.

solve.answer: The gaps between years are unequal, so slopes are distorted
solve.work: Equal spacing for gaps of 1,1,4,4 years distorts slopes.

questions.skill: Judge a summary or picture display
questions.stem: A report says the average salary at a small company is 120 thousand dollars. The five salaries, in thousands of dollars, are 40, 40, 45, 50 and 425. What is the median salary, in thousands of dollars?
questions.solution: The mean is $\frac{40 + 40 + 45 + 50 + 425}{5} = 120$, but one large salary pulls it up. The median, the middle of the ordered values, is 45, which is closer to what most employees earn.

questions.skill: Judge the source of the data
questions.stem: A report on a medicine cites a study in a journal where other scientists reviewed it, and a different report cites testimonials on the maker's webpage. Which is stronger evidence, and why?
choices: The testimonials, because they come from real customers
The testimonials, because they are easier to read
The journal study, because experts checked its methods
The journal study, because journals are expensive
questions.answer: The journal study, because experts checked its methods
questions.solution: A reviewed study has had its methods checked by outside experts. Testimonials on a seller's webpage are chosen by the seller and are not a controlled comparison.

solve.answer: The journal study, because experts checked its methods

questions.skill: Judge a summary or picture display
questions.stem: On a pictograph, a coin icon with a side of 1 centimeter stands for the value in 2012. To show that the value doubled by 2014, the 2014 icon is drawn with a side of 2 centimeters. How many times as large as the 2012 icon is the area of the 2014 icon?
questions.solution: Doubling both the length and the width multiplies the area by $2 \cdot 2 = 4$. The icon looks four times as big, though the value only doubled.

questions.skill: Check a report's claim against its numbers
questions.stem: A drug trial reports, "The drug cut the risk of a stroke by 50%." In the trial, the risk was 4 in 1,000 without the drug and 2 in 1,000 with the drug. How many fewer people per 1,000 had a stroke with the drug?
questions.solution: The risk fell from 4 in 1,000 to 2 in 1,000, which is a 50% drop in relative terms, but the actual difference is $4 - 2 = 2$ people per 1,000.

questions.skill: Check a report's claim against its numbers
questions.stem: A town had 1 case of a disease last year and 3 cases this year. A headline says, "Cases triple!" Which question matters most when judging this headline?
choices: How big the change is compared with the size of the town
Whether the headline uses the word triple in its title
Whether last year had fewer visitors to the town than this year did
What color the graph in the article was printed in
questions.answer: How big the change is compared with the size of the town
questions.solution: A jump from 1 to 3 is tripling in relative terms, but it is only 2 extra cases. To judge its importance, compare the counts with the size of the population and with normal year-to-year variation.

solve.answer: How big the change is compared with the size of the town
solve.work: Tiny counts (1 to 3) relative to town size make "triple" misleading; option about size of change relative to town.

questions.skill: Judge how a sample was chosen
questions.stem: A school mailed a survey to 500 families. Only 100 families replied, and 80 of those replied that they favor a later start time. The report says, "80% of families favor a later start." What is the least possible percent of all 500 families that favor it? Assume the 400 who did not reply could all disagree.
questions.solution: If none of the 400 families that did not reply favors it, then only the 80 who replied yes do. That is $\frac{80}{500} = 0.16$, or 16% of all families. The 80% describes only the 100 who replied.

questions.skill: Judge a study design and its conclusion
questions.stem: A study of cities finds that months with more ice cream sales also have more sunburns. A writer says that ice cream causes sunburns. What is the best explanation of the flaw?
choices: Ice cream sales cannot be counted separately by month
Sunburns are always caused by eating too much ice cream
Cities are far too large to compare with one another
Hot, sunny weather may raise both ice cream sales and sunburns
questions.answer: Hot, sunny weather may raise both ice cream sales and sunburns
questions.solution: A third variable, such as hot sunny weather, can cause both things to rise together. A relationship in data does not show that one variable causes the other.

solve.answer: Hot, sunny weather may raise both ice cream sales and sunburns
solve.work: Lurking variable: hot sunny weather drives both.

questions.skill: Judge a summary or picture display
questions.stem: A report on a treatment says, "Group A: 100% improved. Group B: 60% improved." It does not give the group sizes. Why might the percentages be misleading?
choices: Group A cannot be larger in size than group B is
Group A may be tiny, so 100% could be just 3 of 3 people
Percentages above 50% are never reliable in a report
Group B should have shown an improvement of exactly 100%
questions.answer: Group A may be tiny, so 100% could be just 3 of 3 people
questions.solution: A percentage hides the number of people behind it. A small group can show 100% because of a few people, while a large group's percentage is more dependable.

solve.answer: Group A may be tiny, so 100% could be just 3 of 3 people
solve.work: Without group sizes, 100% may be 3 of 3.

questions.skill: Check a report's claim against its numbers
questions.stem: A product page says its average rating is 4.8 stars, based on only 5 reviews. Four of the reviews are 5 stars. What must the fifth review's star rating be for the average to be 4.8?
questions.solution: The five ratings must add to $4.8 \cdot 5 = 24$. The four 5-star reviews contribute 20, so the fifth is $24 - 20 = 4$ stars. With only 5 reviews, one rating changes the average a lot.

questions.skill: Judge how a sample was chosen
questions.stem: A headline says, "Most teens spend over 5 hours online." It is based on 2,000 volunteers who clicked an ad on a gaming website. Which statement is best supported by the data?
choices: It describes all teens, because 2,000 is such a large number
It describes only gamers, because the ad appeared on a gaming site
It describes the volunteers, who may be heavier users than most teens
It proves that gaming websites cause teens to stay online longer
questions.answer: It describes the volunteers, who may be heavier users than most teens
questions.solution: A large sample does not fix a sample that chose itself. People who click an ad on a gaming site may be unusually heavy users, so the result may not apply to all teens. Nothing here shows that the website causes the hours.

solve.answer: It describes the volunteers, who may be heavier users than most teens
solve.work: Volunteers from a gaming ad are self-selected and possibly heavier users; data describe them only.

questions.skill: Check a report's claim against its numbers
questions.stem: A poll says approval of a mayor rose from 40% to 50%. A headline says, "Approval up 50%!" Which statement is accurate?
choices: Approval rose 10 percentage points, which is a 25% increase
Approval rose 10 percentage points, which is a 50% increase
Approval rose 50 percentage points, which is a 10% increase
Approval rose 25 percentage points, which is a 10% increase
questions.answer: Approval rose 10 percentage points, which is a 25% increase
questions.solution: The rise is $50 - 40 = 10$ percentage points. Relative to the starting 40%, the increase is $\frac{10}{40} = 25\%$. The headline's 50% is not the percent increase.

solve.answer: Approval rose 10 percentage points, which is a 25% increase

questions.skill: Spot a misleading graph axis or scale
questions.stem: Two line graphs sit side by side. One shows company X's revenue on an axis from 0 to 100, and the other shows company Y's on an axis from 0 to 1,000. Both lines reach the same height. What is misleading?
choices: The graphs should have been drawn as pie charts instead
Revenue can never be shown accurately by using only a line graph
Company X's line should end higher than company Y's line
The scales differ, so equal heights hide that Y earns far more
questions.answer: The scales differ, so equal heights hide that Y earns far more
questions.solution: The same height stands for 100 on one graph and 1,000 on the other. Without noticing the axes, a reader would think the companies have equal revenue.

solve.answer: The scales differ, so equal heights hide that Y earns far more
solve.work: Different scales: equal heights hide that Y earns far more.

questions.skill: Judge a study design and its conclusion
questions.stem: One trial gave a new medicine to 6 patients, and 4 improved. Another trial gave it to 600 patients, and 400 improved. Both show about 67% improving. Which trial gives stronger evidence, and why?
choices: The 6-patient trial, because it was easier to carry out and follow
The 600-patient trial, because a larger sample varies less by chance
The 6-patient trial, because fewer of its patients failed to improve
Neither trial, because 67% is not a large enough majority
questions.answer: The 600-patient trial, because a larger sample varies less by chance
questions.solution: With only 6 patients, one or two people changing would change the percentage a lot. A larger sample averages out chance differences, so its percentage is more trustworthy.

solve.answer: The 600-patient trial, because a larger sample varies less by chance
solve.work: Larger sample has less sampling variability, so stronger evidence.
